title: Running a single C# file without a project
hook: Starting with C# 14 and the .NET 10 SDK, you can run one .cs file with dotnet run hello.cs — no .csproj needed. Special #:-prefixed directives at the top of the file act as an inline project file.

blocks.text: A file-based app is a single .cs file that the .NET SDK compiles and runs without a separate project file. You launch it with dotnet run app.cs, dotnet app.cs, or even a Unix shebang (#!/usr/bin/env dotnet). Directives starting with #: at the top of the file configure packages, properties, and SDK — they replace what you would normally put in a .csproj. When the script grows, dotnet project convert app.cs generates a real project.

entries.plainDefinition: A single C# source file that the SDK treats as a complete program without a .csproj on disk.
entries.example: dotnet run probe.cs compiles and executes probe.cs directly.

entries.plainDefinition: A C# 14 line starting with #: that configures the virtual project (packages, properties, SDK).
entries.example: #:package Spectre.Console@* adds a NuGet dependency inline.

entries.plainDefinition: The temporary build configuration the SDK creates in memory for a file-based app.
entries.example: No .csproj file exists on disk, but the build still resolves packages and compiles IL.

blocks.text: File-based apps are perfect for quick spikes: probe a Redis key, parse a Comma-Separated Values (CSV) sample, decode a JSON Web Token (JWT) locally. They are not a replacement for a multi-file worker with tests and CI. Native Ahead-of-Time (AOT) publish is on by default for these apps — great for small tools, but turn it off if you need heavy reflection. Do not place a file-based app inside an existing .csproj tree; MSBuild will pick up the project instead.

blocks.title: When to convert to a project
blocks.body: Run dotnet project convert when you need multiple source files, shared build properties, test projects, or a stable CI pipeline. The language stays C# 14 — only the project structure changes.

blocks.title: From single file to running process

items.title: Write one .cs file with optional #: directives
items.body: Directives declare packages (#:package), properties (#:property), or SDK (#:sdk).

items.title: Run with the SDK
items.body: dotnet run hello.cs creates a virtual project, restores packages, compiles, and executes.

items.title: Top-level statements act as entry point
items.body: Same rules as a normal console app: one file with top-level statements.

items.title: Convert when it grows
items.body: dotnet project convert hello.cs emits a real .csproj and supporting files.

diagram.title: File-based app flow
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  A[Single .cs file] --> B[#: directives]
  B --> C[SDK virtual project]
  C --> D[NuGet restore]
  D --> E[Roslyn compile to IL]
  E --> F[CLR runs entry point]
  A -->|dotnet project convert| G[Real .csproj project]

snippet.label: Minimal file-based app
snippet.explanation: The shebang lets Unix shells run the file directly. #:package pulls Spectre.Console from NuGet. #:property PublishAot=false keeps reflection available.

snippet.label: Common #: directives
snippet.code:
#:sdk Microsoft.NET.Sdk
#:package Newtonsoft.Json@13.0.3
#:property TargetFramework=net10.0
#:property Nullable=enable

Console.WriteLine("configured via directives, not a .csproj");
snippet.explanation: #: directives are SDK configuration — not the classic #if preprocessor. They configure the virtual project the SDK builds in memory.

snippet.label: Run and convert
snippet.code:
# Run directly
dotnet run utility.cs

# Or on Unix with shebang
chmod +x utility.cs
./utility.cs

# Convert to a full project when it outgrows one file
dotnet project convert utility.cs
snippet.explanation: Compare to node file.mjs which runs JavaScript source. dotnet run file.cs still compiles through a virtual project first.

snippet.label: ReadyToRun vs Native AOT directives
snippet.explanation: File-based apps default PublishAot on publish — disable for reflection-heavy scripts. ReadyToRun is a middle ground between pure JIT and full Native AOT.

blocks.title: Single-file scripts
rows: No compile (or tsc first for TS)

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Dating file-based apps to C# 11 because top-level statements arrived earlier — those features are independent. Putting utility.cs inside a csproj directory and wondering why restore picks the project instead of the file. Relying on default PublishAot and then missing a reflection-based serializer.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: file-based apps use an in-memory virtual project — #: directives map to MSBuild properties. dotnet run file.cs uses JIT; dotnet publish file.cs defaults PublishAot for a native binary unless #:property PublishAot=false. ReadyToRun (R2R) via PublishReadyToRun precompiles IL for faster cold start while keeping reflection — useful when full AOT breaks a dependency. Convert to dotnet project convert before adding test projects or complex CI. Shebang scripts need dotnet on PATH — container images must include SDK or published native output.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Dating file-based apps to C# 11 — they are C# 14 / .NET 10 SDK. Assuming #: is preprocessor — it is SDK configuration. Default AOT publish then surprise MissingMethodException from reflection serializer. Keeping a grown multi-file tool as one file because 'file apps are simpler' — convert when CI needs tests.

interviewTakeaways: File-based apps (C# 14, .NET 10) use #: directives as a virtual csproj — dotnet run compiles IL first, unlike node running source.
Publish defaults toward Native AOT; use PublishAot=false or ReadyToRun when reflection or dynamic libraries are required.
In production, convert to a real project before multi-file tests and CI; publish native output for container shebang tools.
60s: dotnet run file.cs with #:package and #:property. Virtual project. Default AOT on publish. R2R middle ground. PublishAot=false for reflection spikes. dotnet project convert when it grows.
Follow-up: how does ReadyToRun differ from Native AOT for a Lambda cold start?
commonPitfalls: Dating file-based apps to C# 11 gets you rejected — C# 14 / .NET 10 SDK feature.
Default PublishAot with reflection-based JSON — runtime failures after publish.
Strong answer: '#: is MSBuild config. AOT for tiny native tools. R2R when reflection needed. Convert for CI and tests.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: node file.mjs runs JavaScript source directly. dotnet run file.cs still compiles through a virtual project then runs. Shebang exists in both ecosystems.
tsx transpiles on the fly without a separate project file. dotnet run file.cs still restores packages and emits IL — closer to tsc plus node with an implicit tsconfig.
